final_answer: Stabilin-2 (HARE) on liver/lymph sinusoidal endothelium is the systemic HA-clearance receptor; Stabilin-1 is mainly a macrophage scavenger receptor with broader expression in immune regulation, not the main HA sink.
note: No evidence window mentions Stabilin-1 at all; the windows cover only Stabilin-2/HARE as the primary scavenger receptor for systemic HA clearance (PMC4839745), so the draft's Stabilin-1 macrophage/immune-regulation contrast is unsettled.

final_answer: Tumors drain through lymphatics; LYVE-1-positive lymphatic endothelium and its HA interactions are implicated in lymphatic invasion and nodal metastasis routes.
note: Evidence PMC6172044 states LYVE-1 is expressed on lymphatic vessel endothelium and that anti-LYVE-1 mAb inhibits cancer metastasis by suppressing lymphangiogenesis; PMC10868962 states lymphangiogenesis is a critical factor in cancer development and metastasis and LYVE-1 overexpression is an adverse prognostic indicator.

final_answer: It associates with microtubules and the mitotic spindle and with ERK complexes, regulating spindle integrity and cell division - functions independent of extracellular HA.
note: Evidence PMC3760809 states RHAMM is a cytoskeletal and mitotic spindle protein that regulates signal transduction at microtubules, specifically ERK1/2 and AURKA, and does not localize to the cell surface; PMC12803952 places HMMR on the mitotic spindle.

final_answer: Hyaluronan-binding protein - typically the aggrecan G1/link-protein complex isolated from cartilage - which binds HA specifically and is biotinylated/labeled for detection.
note: Evidence PMC4234048 states the HABP probe is prepared by enzymatic digestion of aggrecan from bovine nasal cartilage and biotinylated in the presence of bound hyaluronan and the link protein; PMC6078830 describes the biotinylated HABP complex as the aggrecan G1 domain and link protein.

final_answer: The shed CD44 ectodomain, released by metalloproteinase cleavage (e.g., ADAM10, MT1-MMP); it circulates and can act as a decoy for HA binding.
note: Evidence supports CD44 ectodomain cleavage by ADAM10 (PMC2172408) and shedding by MT1-MMP (PMC2174329), but no window states that soluble CD44 circulates or acts as a decoy for HA binding.

final_answer: It is the only known covalent attachment of a protein to HA: inter-alpha-inhibitor heavy chains are transesterified onto HA's GlcNAc residues by TSG-6.
note: Evidence supports the covalent transfer of inter-alpha-inhibitor heavy chains to HA catalyzed by TSG-6 (PMC11325723: 'The covalent transfer of heavy chains from IαI to HA is catalyzed by TsG-6'), but no window states this is the only known covalent protein attachment to HA or that it is a transesterification onto GlcNAc residues.

final_answer: Native HMW-HA (roughly >1000 kDa) is generally anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive, whereas LMW fragments generated during injury/inflammation are pro-inflammatory, signaling via TLR2/TLR4 and CD44.
note: The signaling contrast is supported (PMC3865734: HMW-HA is 'anti-inflammatory, and immunosuppressive' and LMW-HA can initiate inflammatory responses; PMC9138743: LMW-HA pro-inflammatory signaling 'primarily with TLR2 and TLR4'), but no window gives any size figure for HMW-HA, so the draft's 'roughly >1000 kDa' threshold is unsettled.

final_answer: Short HA oligosaccharides (roughly 3–10 disaccharides) are pro-angiogenic, opposite to native HMW-HA, which is anti-angiogenic.
note: Evidence PMC5823590 states: "native high molecular-weight HA (HMW-HA) is anti-angiogenic" whereas "degradation products that are of specific size (e.g., 3–10 disaccharide units; o-HA) exhibit pro-angiogenic activity" — the evidenced oligosaccharide range is 3–10, not the draft's 4-25.

final_answer: Tumor stroma rich in HMW-HA raises interstitial fluid pressure and collapses vasculature; PEGPH20 degrades stromal HA to decompress vessels and improve drug delivery. Its Phase III trial (HALO-301) nevertheless failed to improve overall survival.
note: Evidence supports a dense stroma that can 'compress tumor vasculature' and 'increase interstitial pressure, impeding perfusion' (PMC7499614) and describes HALO-301 as a phase III PEGPH20 trial in hyaluronan-high tumors, but no window states that PEGPH20 degrades stromal HA to decompress vessels or that HALO-301 failed to improve overall survival (only a 'Why HALO 301 Failed' article title appears).

final_answer: SEC-MALS (size-exclusion chromatography with multi-angle light scattering) as the reference method; also gel electrophoresis and intrinsic viscometry.
note: Evidence PMC8433777 states MALS measures absolute MW and 'is usually connected to a chromatographic system', and lists 'viscosimetry, gel, capillary electrophoresis, molecular exclusion chromatography' as other methods; PMC3900495 uses size-exclusion chromatography with multi-angle laser light scattering (SEC-MALS).

final_answer: It depletes the UDP-glucuronic acid substrate pool (via UDP-glucose dehydrogenase competition) and downregulates HAS expression, reducing HA production.
note: Evidence PMC3200435 states: 'It is thought that 4-MU depletes UDP-glucuronic acid (UDP-GlcUA) substrate for HA synthesis and also suppresses HA-synthase expression', in a paper on selective targeting of UDP-glucose dehydrogenase.

final_answer: They make unusually high-MW HA (roughly 6,000-12,000 kDa) due to a distinct HAS2 sequence and very low hyaluronidase activity; removing this HMW-HA abolishes their cancer resistance in experiments.
note: Evidence supports extremely high-MW HA 'over five times larger than human or mouse HA', accumulating due to 'decreased activity of HA-degrading enzymes and a unique sequence of hyaluronan synthase 2 (HAS2)' with a key role in cancer resistance (PMC3720720), but no window gives the 6,000-12,000 kDa range or states that removing this HA abolishes cancer resistance.

final_answer: GPI-anchored HYAL2, cooperating with CD44 at the cell surface, clips HMW-HA into ~20 kDa fragments; these are endocytosed and HYAL1 in lysosomes completes digestion to tetrasaccharides.
note: Evidence supports HYAL2/CD44 roles, initial cleavage at the cell surface, intermediate HA transported to lysosomes for further degradation by HYAL1 (PMC5539311) and 20 kDa HA handling by Hyal1 (PMC7243119), but no window states HYAL2 is GPI-anchored or that digestion is completed to tetrasaccharides.

final_answer: Both its concentration and molecular weight fall (healthy synovial HA is roughly 3-4 mg/mL at several MDa), reducing viscoelasticity - the rationale for viscosupplementation.
note: Evidence supports decreased HA molecular weight and lower concentration in osteoarthritic versus healthy knees (PMC5910459, PMC9797074) and MW ranges of 2.5–7 MDa in non-OA synovial fluid (PMC4721052), but no window gives a healthy concentration of roughly 3-4 mg/mL or states reduced viscoelasticity as the rationale for viscosupplementation.

final_answer: Liver fibrosis/cirrhosis severity (a component of panels such as the ELF test), because hepatic sinusoidal clearance fails as fibrosis progresses.
note: Evidence supports serum HA as one of six biomarkers of liver fibrosis/cirrhosis forming part of the Enhanced Liver Fibrosis (ELF) score (PMC10285560), but no window states that hepatic sinusoidal clearance of HA fails as fibrosis progresses.

final_answer: HAS2 overexpression increases tumor growth/invasion in models, and suppressing HA synthesis (HAS antisense or 4-MU) reduces tumor progression - HA is an active driver, not just a bystander matrix component.
note: Evidence supports HAS2 in CRC malignancy: 'HAS2 depletion increased apoptosis... and decreased EMT-related migration and invasive ability' and 'HAS2 overexpression promoted malignancy features' (PMC6609812), but no window addresses HAS antisense or 4-MU suppressing tumor progression, or tumor growth as such.

final_answer: 4-methylumbelliferone is hymecromone, an approved choleretic/spasmolytic drug in some countries, repurposed experimentally as an HA-synthesis inhibitor.
note: Evidence PMC12139924 states '4-Methylumbelliferone (4-MU) is the active component of hymecromone, a choleretic and antispasmodic drug' approved in Europe and Asia and used to inhibit hyaluronan production; PMC12421109 calls hymecromone 'also known as 4-methylumbelliferone (4-MU)', a small molecule inhibitor of HA synthesis.

final_answer: Reactive oxygen species cleave HA randomly (non-enzymatic scission), giving a broad size distribution; hyaluronidases cut at defined beta(1->4) linkages, giving more uniform oligosaccharide products (ultimately tetrasaccharides for HYAL1).
note: No evidence window discusses reactive oxygen species cleaving HA, random non-enzymatic scission, or the size distribution of ROS products versus hyaluronidase products; the windows only identify bona fide hyaluronidases (HYAL1, HYAL2, SPAM1) as endo-N-acetylhexosaminidases (PMC5363586, PMC7243119).

final_answer: Skin HA content falls markedly with age (by roughly half by about age 50), with epidermal HA disappearing almost entirely in aged skin - a contributor to loss of hydration and turgor.
note: Evidence supports that 'The decrease of epidermal hyaluronic acid content is a hallmark of skin aging' and that aged skin shows loss of hydration and turgor (PMC5871318), but no window quantifies a fall of roughly half by about age 50 or states epidermal HA disappears almost entirely.

final_answer: Cumulus cells synthesize an HA-rich matrix (via HAS2) whose expansion is essential for ovulation/fertilization; HA-based sperm-binding assays exploit mature sperm's HA receptors as a maturity marker.
note: Evidence supports the HA-rich cumulus matrix and Has2 in ovulation: cumulus expansion 'was also shown to be essential not only for ovulation but also for in vivo fertilization' (PMC6396505) and cumulus cells create space 'for accumulation of the hyaluronan-rich matrix' (PMC5805282), but no window mentions HA-based sperm-binding assays or sperm HA receptors as a maturity marker.
